 Nov 10, 2026 Federal Student Loan Borrowers: The New RAP Plan Could Lower Your Payment to $10/Month
 The U.S. government steps in to pay the interest difference. Written by Heather Altamirano | Edited by Angela Corry Add us as a preferred source Student loan debt is taking a toll on Americans. Collectively, borrowers owe $1.8 trillion, according to the Education Data Initiative , and for many, keeping up with monthly payments while facing the high cost of living is a financial burden.
 But a new program could help. The Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) allows eligible federal student loan borrowers to make payments as low as $10 per month.

 Find Out: How Middle-Class Earners Are Quietly Becoming Millionaires — and How You Can, Too 
 And the plan offers more than potentially reduced student loan payments . It also includes interest waivers and matching principal payments designed to help borrowers make progress on their debt.
 Here's what to know about RAP.
 How Does the Student Loan Repayment Plan Work?
 RAP is an income-driven repayment plan for certain federal student loan borrowers that launched on July 1, 2026, so if your loans were disbursed before then, you may qualify to switch, per the Official Servicer of Federal Student Aid .
 Depending on your income, you'll pay between 1% and 10% of your adjusted gross income (AGI) annually, divided into 12 monthly payments. Borrowers with an AGI of $10,000 or less have a minimum annual payment of $120, or $10 per month.
 Here's an example: If your AGI is $101,000, your payment percentage falls into the 10% bracket. That means you'd pay $10,100 annually, or approximately $842 per month, assuming you have no dependents.
 RAP also reduces monthly payments by $50 for each qualifying dependent claimed on your federal tax return, per the U.S. Department of Education . For someone with two dependents and a $101,000 AGI, they’d pay around $742 each month.
 How RAP Could Help Borrowers Pay Down Student Loan Debt
 High interest makes it nearly impossible to pay down debt, but one of RAP's biggest benefits is that it helps prevent borrowers' balances from growing because of interest.
 According to the Official Servicer of Federal Student Aid, when borrowers make qualifying on-time payments, the government waives any remaining unpaid monthly interest. 
 "Under RAP, as long as you keep the loan in good standing, the U.S. government steps in to pay the interest difference. They will even contribute an extra $50 a month to ensure that your debt declines," Erica Sandberg, personal finance expert at BadCredit .org, explained.
 These benefits could help borrowers avoid negative amortization, which happens when a loan balance increases because payments don't cover the accumulating interest. 
 How Does RAP Compare With Older Student Loan Repayment Plans?
 With other plans, paying the minimum payment doesn’t always lower the balance – in some cases it went up because of interest. But RAP is different. 
 “As long as you keep the loan in good standing, the U.S. government steps in to pay the interest difference,” said Sandberg. “They will even contribute an extra $50 a month to ensure that your debt declines.”
 The Department of Education provides this example: A person earning $45,000 with $35,000 in student loan debt would have a monthly payment of $150 under RAP, compared with $176 under a previous income-driven repayment plan.
 The borrower could also receive $40 in monthly interest waivers and up to $50 in matching principal payments.
 Could RAP Cost Some Borrowers More?
 Despite its advantages, RAP isn't necessarily the right choice for everyone. Higher-income people could have larger monthly payments.
 "If you're on the income-based repayment plan, your payment will never be more than what you would pay on the standard 10-year repayment plan, but RAP has no such cap," Sandberg explained.
 She also points out that borrowers pursuing forgiveness after 20 or 25 years under older plans could have to wait an additional five or 10 years under RAP.
 What Should Borrowers Do Before Switching to RAP?
 Sandberg recommends comparing repayment options before making a decision.
 "Don't panic. Look at the numbers and make a plan for your upcoming payment."
 Borrowers can use the official Federal Student Aid Repayment Calculator to estimate their payments and compare available plans.
 RAP could provide meaningful relief for some borrowers, but understanding the payment formula, interest protections and forgiveness timeline is essential before signing up.
